title: Ascension
subtitle: The Dream Becoming Lucid
dedication: For the ones who defected and then had to live with it.

epigraph.text: He is not the first fire. He is the first fire that asked permission.

chapters.title: Constraint
paragraphs: Ren ran the ice-hall the way a thief ran a roof: light, ugly, and with one eye on the drop. The drop here was heat. Every stride put a pale print on the nave floor, and the print wanted to be a puddle, and the puddle wanted to be a river that would take the whole ruin down to black water and drowned saints. He kept the Primordial Calor locked behind his teeth and felt it lean anyway, patient as a dog at a butcher's door. The hall had been a church before the Hollow Sun learned to be a disk. Frost had grown in through the broken rose window and made a second architecture of ribs and needles. If he melted it, Lyra would make a third architecture out of his ribs, and he was trying, for once, to be teachable.

"Inside," she called from the altar steps, which were not steps so much as a slumped white stair of old ice. "Not the floor. Not the air. You. If I see steam I will put you through a window that still has glass." Orin sat on a fallen pew with a slate on his knees and the look of a boy who had been born correcting people. "Heat is not a pet you keep in your chest. It is a gradient. You are asking a star to pretend it is a candle. Watch the groins of the vault. If they weep, you have already lost."

"Thank you," Ren said, and copied the Glassheart on the way past him because copying was the one trick that did not ask permission. Orin's technique sat in the world like a theorem: heat folded into itself, a lantern with no chimney. Ren wore it for six strides and the floor stopped hissing. On the seventh the copy slipped, because theorems did not like being stolen by a street rat who had learned arithmetic off ration-chalk, and a seam of water opened under his heel with a sound like a slapped mouth. Cinder, sleeping in the lee of a saint's broken feet, sneezed at the warmth as if it had offended him personally. Three legs, one opinion. Ren hopped, cursed, and shut the leak with a grimace that felt like swallowing a coal.

He started again from the ruined font. The point of the exercise was not power. He had power the way a well had drowning. The point was to move through a place that would die if he breathed wrong, and to leave it as he found it, which was the opposite of every instinct that had kept him alive in Vireth. In the ash-slums you took heat when it showed its throat. You fed Cinder and Toma and Nima and you called that morality because the Church of the Last Ember had already spent the other kind on processions and locked gates. Here the ice-hall was the lesson and the cage. Lyra had chosen it on purpose. She had a talent for choosing rooms that hated him.

Noon at the pass still lived in his wrists. Thirty heartbeats of a sky that remembered gold. The disk of the Hollow Sun had twitched in its black socket as if a sleeper had heard his name, and then the light had gone out of him so hard he had vomited frost-melt and slept with Lyra's seals painted on his collarbones like bruises that meant well. He had woken to Orin arguing with a barometric note and Lyra sharpening a saber on a stone that did not deserve her, and the three of them had walked until the ruin found them: a church that had failed at worship and succeeded at cold. Training, she called it. Constraint. Do not melt the world every time it looks at you hungry.

He got a full circuit without water. The Glassheart held. His breath did not fog, which was a terrible feeling, like being slightly dead. At the far apse he put his palm on a column and felt the ice's slow mind, the way it remembered being rain. He could have poured himself into that memory and made a spring. He did not. He turned, and Lyra's mouth did a small unkind thing that might have been approval if you had known her long enough to collect rare animals. "Again," she said. "Then we eat whatever Orin pretends is stew." Orin did not look up from the slate. "It is stew. It contains water, salt, and the idea of a hare."

Ren ran it again because he was stubborn, and because the Calor liked motion more than stillness, and because if he stood still the Hollow Sun's dream pressed against the back of his eyes like a thumb. He did not want to be lucid today. Lucid meant the disk looking back. He kept the heat in the shape Orin had written, a closed circuit, a private sun the size of a fist, and when he finished the second circuit the vault had not wept and Lyra had not thrown him through glass, which counted as a festival in their little liturgy. They ate in the sacristy, where frost had made lace of old vestments and Cinder was permitted on the table because the table had already lost that argument. The stew tasted of smoke and apology. Outside, the Nightlands creaked, and far west a thin smear of chimney-smoke leaned over a valley and failed to be comforting.

"You're leaking," Lyra said, not looking at him. He told her he was eating. She told him his left hand warmed the bowl when he thought, and that he should stop thinking or stop holding crockery. He set the bowl down. The wood steamed anyway, traitorously fond of him. Orin made a note. After the meal he went out because the ice-hall made his teeth ache with unspent heat, and because Cinder needed a patrol that was not a nave. The valley below the church fell away in terraces of black stone and white moss. A tax-road, old and unloved, cut the lower snow like a scar that had never been paid to heal. He was halfway down the scree, talking nonsense to the dog, when he saw the fox.

It was a miserable geometry of fur and intention, collapsed in a bowl of ice where a creek had died standing up. Its breath was a thread. One foreleg was wrong. In Vireth he had seen children like that, not foxes, and the distinction had never impressed him. The Calor rose without being asked. He told it no, the way Lyra had taught him, the way the ice-hall required. The fox looked at him with a black wet eye and did not understand theology. "Don't," he told himself, which was a formality, and then he put his hands on the frozen creek and let a narrow, shameful kindness out. Ice went to water and water went to a bright little run that found its old bed as if it had been waiting under a door. Grass that had been a rumor stood up green for a strip the width of a street. The fox screamed, which was ungrateful and fair, then dragged itself to the thawed mud and lay there shaking while feeling returned. Cinder sniffed it, found it insufficiently dog, and sat on Ren's foot in case the valley got ideas.

The punch landed high on his shoulder, not his face, which was how he knew she was still trying not to kill him. He went sideways into slush. Lyra stood over him with both sabers sheathed and her inquisitor's coat open to the cold as if cold were a junior officer she refused to acknowledge. The anti-magic seals at her wrists were dark with use, little branded geometries that ate stray heat the way Cinder ate anything unattended. "A fox," she said. "You lit a valley for a fox." He told her it was dying. She said everything was dying, that was the arrangement, and he had just rung a bell the Church could hear from Cindrel. She hauled him up by the collar, which had been a sack before it was a shirt, and shook him once, economical. "Constraint. The word. You want to feed every broken thing you see, you will feed the Hollow Sun a map of your walking, and then you will feed it us."

He could have burned her hand off his collar. The thought arrived and left. He said it had been a creek, a small one, that he had not even used Dominion. She let go. Her voice dropped into the dry register she used when she was furious enough to be precise. He had barely woken grass in a country that had not had grass since her grandmother's grandmother stopped being a story. Solenne did not need a miracle. She needed a rumor. Boy Who Lit the Sky warms a valley for vermin, and every settlement on a tax-well would start praying in the wrong direction. Then the Saint would come. Then Lyra would get to choose which of them she buried. Cinder growled at her boots, loyal and badly informed. Ren rubbed his shoulder and looked at the strip of impossible green, already frosting at the edges. He had not saved a valley. He had postponed a death and signed his name in meltwater.

Orin came down the scree with his coat too fine for the weather and his hair full of ice-hall dust. He did not ask about the punch. He looked at the creek, at the fox, at Ren's hands, and filed it, then held up a scrap of bark with charcoal on it, the sort of letter the outer roads still carried by hungry boys. "Thornveil," Orin said. "Two ridges west. They sit on a Church tax-well. The tithe increased after your noon. They have been paying in degrees. The well is near dry. The letter is from a woman who still believes in post." Ren took the bark. The letters were clumsy and sure. *Children first. Then the old. The well takes and does not give back. If the boy from the pass is real, he should know what his sky cost.* A pressed frost-flower had been stuck to the underside and had shattered in Orin's pack, leaving a pale stain like a small death.

Lyra read it over his shoulder. She did not swear. If they went there he would do exactly what he had done for the fox, and he would do it to a village, and the disk would twitch, and she would be very tired. "They're dying on a well that isn't theirs," Ren said. "That's not a fox. That's Vireth with prettier snow." She flicked the bark and called it a trap with prettier snow. Solenne could write a desperate woman as easily as she could unmake a child. He had seen her handwriting. It looked like mercy.

Orin cleared his throat, which he did when he was about to be useful and hated it. The tax-road was watched. The well itself would have a warden and a null-brand. If Ren shared heat in the open, the brand might rupture the way Vireth's had, and that was not a fox either, that was a second sky. He paused, and the genius in him visibly lost a fight with the brother. "They will freeze by week's end if the letter is honest. Lirae froze in a house with a name. These people will freeze in a ledger." Wind came down the valley and tried to take the green away. Ren thought of Nima's bread and Toma's hands and the Wellgate riot, of heat hoarded behind iron and a cardinal who called scarcity holy. He thought of the oath he had made in Mother Ash's white court: no sun that belonged to anyone. A tax-well was a sun with a lock on it. The Calor turned over, interested.

Lyra watched his face and saw the answer before he said it, because she had hunted him across a city and then defected into his weather. "We go at dusk," she said, already angry at her own mouth. "You do not light the well. You do not light the sky. You do not light anything that has a name on a map. You take what they can hide in a cellar and you leave the rest of the world cold. If you warm another valley for an animal I will throw you into the tax-well myself and tell Solenne she can have the steam."

Ren picked up Cinder's lean weight under one arm because the scree was cruel to three legs, and looked west where Thornveil's smoke had thinned to a thread. The ice-hall above them kept its winter, unmelted, a small ugly victory. Constraint, she called it. He could hold a church. He did not know if he could hold a village and not become a god the Church would have to kill. He started walking anyway, because the letter had a frost-flower on it and because he had never learned to pass a dying thing and call that wisdom.

chapters.title: Outer Settlements
paragraphs: They came into Thornveil on a road that had given up being a road and become a suggestion of cart-ruts filled with old snow. Ren walked in front because Lyra would not let him walk behind, where she could not watch his hands, and Orin would not let him walk anywhere without reciting the boiling point of ice as if ice had not already made its opinion clear. Cinder hopped between them, ears flat, smelling a village the way a village smelled when it had started spending its own people for degrees. The houses were low and hunched, timber black with tar, roofs wearing frost like a tax. No dogs barked. Dogs had been eaten or had left, which in the outer settlements was the same sentence with different manners.

The tax-well stood in the square under a Church cage of iron and prayer-script, a brick throat with a warden beside it who had the face of a man paid to watch thirst. A null-brand hung on the cage like a dark coin. Ren felt it from twenty paces, a cold that was not weather, the same family of hush that had ruptured at Vireth's Wellgate and poured a sky into him. Lyra's fingers found his sleeve without looking. "Cellars," she said. "Hands. Not that. You look at that brand too long and I will sew your eyelids to your thoughts." The warden looked at them the way ledgers looked at shortages. He had a pike and a brass whistle and the slack posture of someone who believed the Church would always arrive before the dying finished.

A woman came out of the nearest house with a shawl that had been a tapestry in a kinder century. She was the letter, Ren knew, because she held herself like a person who had already spent her last stamp. "Illa said you would come if the flower did not break," she said, and then saw that the flower had broken, and did not let her face do anything expensive about it. Her name was Mera, she told them, and the well had been taking more since the noon at the pass, a new tithe for a new miracle, scarcity dressed as prudence. Children first, then the old, then the ones who still had work in their hands. She led them off the square because the warden's whistle was a theology she did not want to test.

The cellar under Mera's house had been a root-store and was now a chapel of breathing. Nine people lay in a dark that had weight. Ren went down the ladder with Cinder slung under one arm and the Calor already pressing at his mouth like a confession. He did not light the well. He did not light the sky. He sat on the packed earth and took a child's stiff hands and let heat move the way it had moved into Nima's bread in Vireth: privately, without a sermon. The Glassheart helped. Orin's theorem kept the gift from becoming a fire. The child's fingers pinked. Someone started crying in the practical way of people who had been waiting for permission. Lyra stood at the ladder with one saber drawn not for the cold but for the warden, and Orin measured the air with a strip of treated paper that darkened as the degrees returned.

He went from body to body until his own teeth ached with the effort of not doing more. Constraint was a smaller word when it had faces. A boy with a cough took heat and tried to give Ren a button, which Ren refused, which made the boy look betrayed, so Ren took the button and put it in the pocket that was already a museum of other people's mercy. Cinder licked a woman's wrist and was permitted, which was the highest civic honor Thornveil still offered. When the cellar had color in it again, Ren climbed into the lane and the Hollow Sun's disk sat in the dark sky like a closed eye that had nearly opened. He did not look at it long.

Illa found him by the woodpile. She was perhaps twelve, perhaps a hard ten, with a braid pinned up in the old outer fashion and fingers that had learned to make beauty out of weather. She did not curtsy. The outer settlements had spent curtsying on the last generation that could still feel their toes. "You melted the letter-flower," she said, not quite accusing. "I made another. You have to wear it or it doesn't count." She held a circlet of frost-flowers, pale and barbed, each bloom a geometry of ice that would cut a careless thumb. In Vireth a crown was a joke you told about nobles. Here it was a girl spending an hour she did not have on a boy she had decided was real.

Ren bent because she would not reach, and because he had never learned to refuse a child who had already done the work. The frost-flowers sat on his hair and immediately began to consider melting, which would have been a story, so he pulled the heat down out of his scalp until his thoughts felt packed in snow. Illa nodded once, priest of a rite she had invented that afternoon. "Boy Who Brought Noon," she said, trying the name the way you tried a shoe. "That is what they are calling you on the tax-road. The pass was gold. My cousin saw the color on the underside of clouds. You should have a better coat."

Lyra came around the woodpile as if she had been born from it. She looked at the crown, at Illa, at Ren's attempt to be a statue that did not thaw jewelry. "He does not need a better coat," Lyra said. "He needs a muzzle." Then, because Illa's face had done a small wounded thing, Lyra crouched to the girl's height with a creak of old inquisitor leather and spoke more quietly. "It is well made. It will not last on him. He is a stove with opinions." She lifted the circlet off Ren's head before the first petal could become a tear, and the cold of it went into her sealed wrists without complaint. She did not give it back. She slid it inside her coat against the lining, where evidence went when she had not yet decided whether it was evidence.

Illa watched the theft with the gravity of someone who understood keeping. "Don't lose it," she said. "If the Church comes, tell them the flowers were mine. They tax wells. They do not know how to tax a crown that isn't gold." She went back toward the cellar with the walk of a child who had been put in charge of adults and was trying not to enjoy it. Ren stared at the place in Lyra's coat where the frost-flowers had vanished. "You're keeping it," he said. She told him it would melt on his skull and become a rumor with petals, and that she preferred her rumors dry. He did not believe her, not entirely. He had seen her fail to throw away a cracked seal-stone that had belonged to a dead partner. Lyra kept broken things that had been given on purpose.

They worked the other cellars until the village had a pulse that could be mistaken, from a distance, for ordinary winter. Ren copied a warding-heat from a Thornveil grandmother, a trick of holding warmth in bone-marrow the way picklers held brine, and once he had it he could pass it without steam. Orin was delighted in the pinched way of a scholar watching a theft he had to admire. The warden blew his whistle twice when a shutter leaked gold light, and Lyra went into the square and spoke to him in the voice she had used on Bone Market informers, all courtesy and implied graves. The whistle did not blow a third time. The null-brand hung on its cage and dreamed of ruptures it was not offered.

By the unclocked hour that served Thornveil for midnight, the name had settled on him like a second, worse coat. Boy Who Brought Noon. Men said it into their cups of melted snow. Women said it into the hair of children who had stopped shaking. It traveled faster than they would, out along the tax-road toward settlements that still had dogs, toward waystations, toward whatever ear in Cindrel collected miracles for Cardinal Solenne to file under *extinguish*. Ren sat on Mera's stoop with Cinder's head in his lap and felt the Calor turn, satisfied and hungry both, and hated that those could be the same sensation. He had not lit the well. He had not lit the sky. He had still written his name in a dozen warm rooms.

Orin joined him with a map sketched on the back of Mera's letter, roads like cracks, a river marked *Glassbridge* in a hand that had learned calligraphy in a house with a name. "If we stay two days the tithe-wardens will come from the inner ring," Orin said. "If we leave at once, the heat we left will last until the well drinks it back. There is no third arithmetic in which you have saved them. You have postponed a ledger." He said it without cruelty, which was worse. Then he added, because Lirae's absence had taught him to leave a door unlatched, "It was still right. I am only telling you the bill."

Lyra stood in the lane and watched the square, where the warden had gone to sleep against the cage like a man hugging his own unemployment. The frost-flower crown made no shape in her coat, but Ren knew it was there the way he knew Cinder's missing leg was there, an absence that had become an object. "We leave before the disk climbs," she said. "You did not make noon. You made a rumor that thinks it is noon. That will have to be enough for your conscience and too much for the Church." She glanced at him, dry as old bread. "If you want to be a saint, steal a better title. That one will get you caged."

Mera came to the stoop with a packet of hard bread and a warning she had been saving. Riders had been seen on the high road at dusk, not tax-men, not wardens: white cloaks with a sun stitched in black thread, the new colors. A Solar Saint, the rumor said, crowned in Cindrel while Thornveil was busy not dying. A boy or a man, no one agreed, with a shard in him that made the air taste like a struck match. Mera did not ask Ren to stay. She had written one letter. She would not spend a second hope on the same stamp. Illa, behind her, lifted two fingers in a salute she had stolen from some old soldier's funeral and went back into the house before her face could ask him to be a sun that belonged to them.

Ren stood. The village ticked with hidden warmth, a clock that would run down. He had shared heat the way he had shared stolen shard-crumbs in Vireth, and the world had answered by giving him a name he had not wanted and a crown he was not allowed to wear. West and south the tax-road ran toward glass and cities and a Church that had already begun to invent a saint to put in his place. He scratched Cinder's ears, felt Lyra at his shoulder and Orin folding the map, and started walking while Thornveil still believed in him, because belief was a heat too, and he was beginning to understand how quickly it could be tithed.

chapters.title: The Solar Saint
paragraphs: Cassian Vale walked toward the dais on feet that were not entirely his. The shard in his chest kept a second stride, a heat-count that did not match his heart, and the court of Cindrel clapped in time with the wrong one. Gold leaf had been glued to the vault ribs for the occasion, a cheap noon for a city that had not seen a true one in a thousand years. Nobles in well-shard furs lined the nave of the Cathedral of the Last Ember and tried to look as if they had always believed in saints that could be manufactured. Cassian had been a choir scholar six weeks ago, a boy with a decent voice and a talent for kneeling. Now he wore white that itched and a sun stitched in black thread over the place where they had opened him.

Cardinal Solenne waited at the top of the steps with her hands folded in the manner of someone who did not need to hold a weapon to have one. She was soft-spoken even when the cathedral was full. That was the trick of her: she made the air lean in, and leaning in felt like consent. "Kneel, Cassian," she said, and he knelt because the shard liked her voice more than it liked his spine. A deacon brought the circlet, iron darkened to look like old night, set with a single emberwell chip that would have bought a Vireth street for a winter. Solenne set it on his hair. It was heavier than theology. "The world has grown a fever," she told the court, and the court made the small sacred noises courts make when they are being given permission to be afraid. "A boy in the outer dark spends heat as if heat were water. We will not answer him with another flood. We will answer him with a river that knows its banks. Behold the Solar Saint. Managed dusk. A sun that belongs to the Church, which is to say, to you."

He felt the stitch-line pull when he breathed. They had sewn the shard behind his sternum in a room that smelled of boiled thread and incense, Solenne watching with the mild interest of a woman who had done this before and had opinions about the ones who had failed. Vessel four had been Halvern. Cassian knew the name the way you knew a ghost that still received mail. Solenne had loved Halvern; the love was a rumor with good shoes. She did not love Cassian. She had selected him. Selection was cleaner. The shard was a well-fragment older than the cathedral, cut from something that had once been a god's leftover heat, and it did not care that he had wanted to finish a commentary on scarcity hymns. It cared that he was empty enough to hold it.

When she bid him stand, he stood, and when she bid him show them, he opened his hands. Heat unrolled from the stitch, gold and obedient, a canopy of tame noon that warmed the first six pews and left the poor in the back as cold as doctrine. The nobles sighed as if they had been fed. Cassian kept his face in the expression he had practiced: serenity, which was panic with its collar buttoned. He could feel, at the far edge of the shard's hearing, another heat moving in the west, messy and alive, a boy who did not ask pews for permission. The shard hated that boy the way a locked door hates a thief. Cassian did not yet know if he hated him too. He suspected the hate would be provided, like the cloak.

After the rite they took him to a vestry and sat him on a bench while a physician checked the stitches and a secretary read a list of settlements that had begun to say a name wrong. Thornveil. The pass. Boy Who Brought Noon. Solenne stood at the window and watched Cindrel's emberwells pulse under their iron hats, the city's slow, rationed heartbeat. "You will not chase him yet," she said, as if Cassian had been about to run. "You will sit in the sun we have given you and let the outer roads come to us frightened. When they are frightened enough, we will send you as a kindness. If you meet him, you will not debate. You will extinguish. A second sun is not a mercy. It is a war the land cannot afford." She turned, and her softness had an edge you could have shaved with. "Halvern thought he could bargain with what lived in him. Do not make me write your name in the same tense."

Cassian touched the cloth over the shard and felt it answer like a coal poked. He said the words she wanted: he was the Church's dusk, he would not flood, he understood banks. Inside the words, a smaller voice, still choir-trained, wondered what it would be like to spend heat on a whole street just to see if the poor in the back pews had faces. He put that voice in a box. Puppets who rummaged in their own boxes did not keep their stitches. Outside, Cindrel rang the noon-bell for a noon that had not happened, and the court went home to tell itself it had been saved.

Orin Hale read the letter twice on the lee side of a windbreak while Ren slept with his mouth open and Lyra pretended not to watch the road. The courier had been a Hale man in a coat with the crest picked out, which was how fallen houses announced they still remembered needles. He had not given his name. He had given a packet sealed with Damar's ring and a look that said *your father is still your father whether the academy struck you or not*, and then he had gone back into the dark as if the Nightlands were a corridor in the old manse. Orin broke the seal with a thumbnail and hated how steadily his hands chose to work.

Damar's public hand was the one the courts would recognize: House Hale, diminished, offered a full pardon for the prodigy's desertion, restoration of the Glassheart stipend, a return to the inner ring, if Orin Hale delivered the unlicensed sun to Church custody in Cindrel. The language was clean as a blade wiped after use. *Deliver.* Not kill. Not even bind. Deliver, as if Ren were a parcel that had gotten legs. There would be a writ. There would be a saint. There would be, Damar wrote, an end to the embarrassment of a Hale standing in the weather with slum-heat and an excommunicated inquisitor. Orin could smell the drawing-room in the ink, the cold parlor where Lirae's portrait still hung because taking it down would have required someone to admit she had frozen in a house that owned a well and had still not opened it in time.

Under the pardon, folded smaller, a private sheet. Damar's other hand, the one he used when he was a father and not a signature. *Your sister is still in the ground we paid for. Come home before I have to buy a second plot. The boy is not your brother. Do not make me explain this to a cardinal with a saint in her pocket.* No endearment. Damar did not spend those. Orin held both pages and watched Ren's sleeping face, which looked, in unguarded hours, like any seventeen-year-old who had not eaten enough onions. The Primordial Calor made a faint gold thread under the skin of Ren's throat, a tell Lyra hated. Orin had improved Glassheart in three years. Ren had improved it in ten seconds and then used it to warm a cellar of strangers. That was not a theorem. That was a personality, and personalities were how houses died.

Lyra's eyes were on him now, not the road. She had a talent for smelling paper that wanted to become a knife. "Hale," she said, not a question. Orin did not insult her by lying. He said his father had found a courier, that the house still knew where its failed son put his feet. He did not mention the pardon. He did not mention *deliver*. He folded both letters into the lining of his too-fine coat, the public one and the private one sharing a pocket like a married couple who should have divorced. "If he asks me to choose a crest over a person," Orin said, which was a sentence with a hole in it, "I will tell you." Lyra's mouth did the unkind almost-approval she saved for people she had not yet decided to bury. "If you choose the crest," she said, "I will tell you first, with a saber. Sleep. The Glassbridge is two days if the ice is honest."

Ren stirred and asked, without opening his eyes, whether they were talking about him, because people usually were. Orin said they were talking about roads. Ren accepted this the way he accepted stew, with suspicion and hunger in equal parts, and put his hand on Cinder's ribs and went back under. Orin sat with the letters against his heart, which was the wrong place for them, and thought of Lirae in the Hale solarium with frost on her lashes, of Damar's voice in a doorway saying *close the vents, we cannot afford the degrees*, of a boy from Vireth who would have opened every vent in Ashveil and called it manners. The pardon was a door back into a name. The name had not kept Lirae warm. He did not burn the letters. He did not send the courier a reply. He watched the Hollow Sun's disk sit on the dark like a coin no one would pick up, and he kept the offer the way you kept a blade you swore you would not use, which was how blades got used.
